title: Light falloff — Image Wiki
text:
Light falloff
  How fast light gets dimmer as it travels away from its source. The useful part is that it changes fastest right next to the lamp and barely at all far away.

  
    Termlight falloff
    Also calledinverse square law, light decay, distance falloff
    Not the same ashard and soft light, light intensity, exposure
    Read9 min
  

  
    
      On this page
      
        Why it happensWhat it does inside one faceWhat it does to the backgroundThe other end of the curveWhat you can see in the pictureCommon mistakes
      
    
  

  Light a face with a phone screen in a dark room and the far cheek disappears; light it with the noon sun and nothing dims at all, out to the grass fifty metres off. The sun being more powerful is not the difference. The difference is falloff: how much dimmer the light gets between one point in the scene and the next. Light direction tells you which way light comes from; falloff tells you how far it survives.
Why it happens
Light leaves a small source in all directions and spreads over an expanding sphere. That is the inverse square law, and that is all of it.

d · 100%2d · 25%3d · 11%One bundle, three distancestwice as far, four times the area, a quarter the light3 stops gone1.2 stops¼ stop100%75%50%25%0.5 m2 m5 m10 mwhere you already areThe same one-metre stepshare of the light you keep after taking it

Left: follow a single bundle of rays outward. At d it lands on one square. At 2d the same bundle is spread across four of them, at 3d across nine — so each square receives a quarter, then a ninth, of what it got at d, which is why the panels are drawn progressively darker. Nothing is absorbed on the way out; the light is only thinned.
Right: the same law read as a rate, which is the form you actually use. The curve is the share of your light that survives one further metre of distance. Half a metre from a lamp, one step costs three stops. Ten metres out, the same step costs a quarter of a stop. The law has not changed — only where you are standing on the curve.


What matters in practice is the rate of dimming, and that depends entirely on where you already are. The same one-metre move:

So a lamp in a small room is a precision instrument; outdoors in sun, distance is irrelevant — from 150 million kilometres out, crossing a field changes nothing.
What it does inside one face
Put a desk lamp 40 cm from someone's near cheek; the far cheek is maybe 60 cm out. (40 ÷ 60)² = 0.44, so the far side of one head gets less than half the light — over a stop across a single face. Move the lamp back to three metres and the cheeks sit at 3.0 m and 3.2 m: a 13% difference, invisible.
Cambridge in Colour puts the same thing as a percentage: the far side of a subject sits 5% further from a distant light, 50% further from a close one. A close source lights unevenly by definition, and no exposure fixes it, because both sides are in one frame.



Georges de La Tour, The Magdalen with the Smoking Flame, c. 1640. One candle, and it is close — so this is falloff at its most extreme. Public domain.
Follow the light outward from the flame. The books and the skull sitting beside it are blazing. Her hands, maybe twice as far, are already dimmer. Her shoulder and the folds of the sleeve behind it drop further again, and the wall a metre back is simply gone. Nothing here is painted black because it is a dark object; the wall is presumably an ordinary wall. It is dark because it is far from a small flame.





Joseph Wright of Derby, A Philosopher Giving that Lecture on the Orrery, in which a Lamp is put in place of the Sun, c. 1766 (Derby Museum and Art Gallery). Public domain.
The single source is the lamp standing in for the sun inside the machine, hidden behind the silhouetted boy at the centre. It is a distance ladder, and you can rank four rungs of it by eye alone.
Start at the two children leaning over the brass rings: nearest the lamp, and so bright their cheeks are near white. Step back to the lecturer in the red robe, further out and clearly duller though he faces the lamp squarely. Step back again to the man taking notes at the left, dimmer still. Then the bookcase in the top right corner, where a few spines catch just enough to be legible.
Nothing in that sequence is a darker object than the one before it. The only thing that changed along the way is distance — and this is the same fact the diagram states as a curve, with the lamp deliberately hidden so that only its effect is visible.


What it does to the background
The Strobist demonstration is worth carrying around. A subject stands 45 cm from an umbrella, 1.8 m in front of a white wall. The wall is five times further from the light, so it gets roughly 1/25 as much — four and a half stops down — and expose for the face and it goes almost black. Pull the light back to three metres and the ratio drops under a stop: the same wall returns as light grey.



Alfred T. Palmer, riveter at the Vultee-Nashville aircraft plant, Tennessee, February 1943. Library of Congress FSA/OWI Collection. Public domain.
The photograph the paragraph above describes, taken in a factory. She and the aluminium panel under her hands are fully exposed; two metres past her the building has gone black.
The important part is what is in that black. Look along the left edge and at the top: an air hose, a chain, some framing, faintly legible. The space is there and it is an ordinary lit factory — it is simply much further from the lamp than she is, so it lands four or five stops down and photographs as nothing. A dark background tells you very little about the room a photograph was taken in.


The other end of the curve



John Constable, The Hay Wain, 1821 (National Gallery, London). Public domain.
The same law, read from the flat end. Pick the sunlit grass on the near bank, then the sunlit meadow beyond the trees, then the field at the horizon perhaps half a mile away. They are the same brightness, and the pale figures out in that far meadow on the right are lit as strongly as the cart standing in the foreground water.
The source here is the sun and the whole sky, and nothing in the scene is measurably closer to either. Distance in this picture is carried by haze, by detail and by colour — never by dimming, because there is no dimming available. A lamp would have run out of light before the second tree.


What you can see in the picture

A brightness gradient across a plain flat surface with no object causing it. Steep means a close source.
A difference between the near and far side of one object, on top of the light-and-shade pattern of The anatomy of a shadow.
A background far darker than the subject with nothing else explaining it — used deliberately, the cheapest way to separate subject from surroundings (Value structure).
Or the opposite: every depth equally lit, meaning a source that is very far, very large, or the sun.


Falloff is not softness
Moving a light changes two unrelated things at once. Falloff is intensity versus distance: how much dimmer things get as they recede from the lamp. Softness is apparent size: how wide the source looks from the subject (Hard and soft light).
To keep them apart: back away from a lamp and the light reaching you drops with the square of the distance, but the lamp does not look dimmer — its apparent area shrinks by the same factor, so its surface brightness is unchanged. It looks smaller, not darker. Smaller is hardness; less light arriving is falloff.

Dave Walvoord, lighting How to Train Your Dragon, uses falloff as a depth tool: a close light pushes near and far characters apart, a distant one flattens them into one plane. In a renderer it is a decay setting, and sun-type lights usually have none.
Common mistakes

"Inverse square means light dies quickly." Close to the lamp, brutally; past a few metres it is nearly flat. The law is a ratio between two distances, not an absolute range.
"The sun doesn't obey the inverse square law." It does. You stand far out on the curve, where it is flat.
"It got harder when I moved it back, so hardness made it dimmer." Two separate effects arriving together. See Hard and soft light.
"A wall gets darker as I walk away from it." No. Falloff applies from lamp to wall, not wall to eye. A surface keeps its brightness at any viewing distance, which is why a distant white building still looks white.
"Bright near side and black far side of one face is a bad exposure." It is a close source. Move the lamp back, do not change the exposure.


How to read falloff in five seconds

Find the brightest point. Is there a source there, or just off-frame in that direction?
Follow one continuous flat surface away from that point. Does it dim, and how fast?
Compare the near and far side of one object. A big drop across a head means a source a metre or two away.
Check the background tone against the distance you would guess. Pitch black right behind a subject standing next to a lit wall is a contradiction.
If a lamp is visible, look at the surface around it. A real lamp leaves a bright pool that fades fast; one sitting on an evenly lit wall is worth flagging.
